title: Design a Web Crawler
summary: You'll be able to design a polite, distributed web crawler: the URL frontier, robots.txt, URL normalization, Bloom-filter and content dedup, trap defenses, and the throughput and memory math.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a crawler to be **polite**, and what is `robots.txt`?
questions.hint: Think about the website owner's servers and wishes.
keyPoints: Politeness means not overloading any single host: limit to about one connection per host and wait between requests
Honor a Crawl-delay or slow down when a site responds slowly or returns 429/503
robots.txt is a file at the site root (/robots.txt) listing paths crawlers may not fetch (Disallow), per user agent
The crawler fetches and caches robots.txt per host before crawling it and checks every URL against it
It is a convention (Robots Exclusion Protocol, RFC 9309), not access control
questions.answer:
A **polite** crawler never overloads any one website. The site belongs to someone else, and a crawler at 800 pages/s could easily knock a small server over (and get itself blocked).

Politeness in practice:
- **One connection per host**, with a pause between requests (e.g. 1 s).
- Honor a site's `Crawl-delay` if given, and **slow down** when the site responds slowly or returns `429 Too Many Requests` or `503 Service Unavailable`.

**`robots.txt`** is a plain text file at the root of a site (`https://example.com/robots.txt`) where the owner lists, per **user agent** (crawler name), which paths crawlers should not fetch:

```text
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Crawl-delay: 2
```

The crawler fetches `robots.txt` **before** crawling a host, caches it (about a day), and checks every URL against its rules before fetching.

It is a **convention** (the Robots Exclusion Protocol, standardized as RFC 9309), not security: nothing stops a rude crawler from ignoring it, so real access control needs authentication.

questions.prompt: Your crawler will see about **4 billion** distinct URLs. Size a Bloom filter for the URL-seen check with a **0.1%** false-positive rate. How many bits per URL, how much memory, and how many hash functions? What does a false positive cost the crawler?
keyPoints: Memory = 4e9 × 14.4 bits ≈ 5.75e10 bits ≈ 7.2 GB
Hash functions k = 14.4 × 0.693 ≈ 10
A false positive makes the crawler think an unseen URL was seen, so that page is skipped (missed), not crawled twice
Bloom filters have no false negatives, so a seen URL is never re-added
questions.answer:
```text
m/n = -ln(0.001) / (ln 2)^2 = 6.908 / 0.4805 ≈ 14.4 bits per URL
m   = 4e9 × 14.4 ≈ 5.75e10 bits ≈ 7.2 GB
k   = 14.4 × ln 2 ≈ 9.97 → 10 hash functions
```
A false positive means ~0.1% of genuinely new URLs are wrongly skipped. No URL is ever crawled twice because of the filter (no false negatives).

questions.prompt: You must crawl **3 billion pages per month**. Average page size is **80 KB** and an average fetch takes **1.5 s**. Estimate (a) pages per second on average, (b) concurrent in-flight fetches at a 2× peak, (c) raw storage per month, (d) average download bandwidth.
questions.hint: A month is about 2.6 million seconds. Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × latency.
keyPoints: Average rate = 3e9 / 2.59e6 ≈ 1,160 pages/s
Peak ≈ 2,300 pages/s; in flight = 2,300 × 1.5 s ≈ 3,500 concurrent fetches (Little's Law)
Storage = 3e9 × 80 KB = 240 TB/month raw (less after compression)
Bandwidth = 1,160 × 80 KB ≈ 93 MB/s ≈ 740 Mbps average
Notes that concurrency is achievable with async I/O across a handful of machines and that politeness, not raw bandwidth, limits per-site speed

questions.prompt:
Write `normalizeUrl(raw, base)` for the crawler's dedup step. It should resolve relative links against `base`, lowercase the scheme and host, drop default ports, remove the `#fragment`, remove query parameters starting with `utm_`, and sort the remaining query parameters. Return `null` for anything that isn't `http` or `https` (e.g. `mailto:`).

Example: `normalizeUrl("../b?z=1&utm_source=x&a=2#top", "HTTP://Example.com:80/x/y/")` → `"http://example.com/x/b?a=2&z=1"`.
questions.hint: The built-in `URL` class handles resolution, case, default ports and dot segments. `url.searchParams` has `delete` and `sort`.
keyPoints: Uses new URL(raw, base) to resolve relative URLs, lowercase scheme/host, drop default ports and resolve ../
Returns null for non-http(s) protocols and for unparseable input (try/catch)
Clears the fragment (url.hash = '')
Removes utm_* parameters without skipping any while iterating (collect keys first)
Sorts remaining query parameters (searchParams.sort()) and returns url.href

questions.prompt: Your crawler now runs on **100 machines**. How do you split the work so that the per-host politeness rule (at most one request per second per host) still holds, and what happens when one machine dies?
questions.hint: Who should own a given host's queue?
keyPoints: Partition by host (hash of hostname), not by URL, so every URL of a host lands on the same worker
Use consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) so adding/removing machines moves only ~1/N of hosts
Each worker enforces politeness locally with per-host queues and a next-allowed-time heap; no cross-machine coordination per request
Discovered links for hosts owned elsewhere are forwarded (in batches) to the owning worker
When a worker dies, its hosts move to ring neighbors and its frontier is recovered from durable storage/log; in-flight URLs may be refetched (acceptable, idempotent)
questions.answer:
**Partition by host, not by URL.** Each URL goes to the worker that owns `hash(hostname)`, so every URL of `example.com` lands on the same machine. If URLs were spread randomly, 100 machines could each hit `example.com` once a second and politeness would be gone.

**Use consistent hashing with virtual nodes** (each machine gets many points on the ring, which evens out the load). Adding or removing a machine then moves only about 1/N of the hosts (~1% with 100 machines) instead of reshuffling everything.

**Politeness stays local.** Each worker keeps one queue per host it owns and a min-heap of hosts ordered by `next_allowed_at`. It pops the host that is ready soonest, fetches one URL, and sets `next_allowed_at = now + 1 s`. No cross-machine coordination per request.

**Forward foreign links.** When worker 7 extracts a link to a host owned by worker 42, it buffers it and sends URLs in **batches** (say every second or every 1,000 URLs) to cut network overhead.

**When a machine dies:** failure detection removes it from the ring; its hosts move to ring neighbors. The new owners rebuild those hosts' frontier queues from **durable storage** (e.g. a replicated log or checkpointed frontier). Some URLs that were in flight get fetched again, which is fine: a fetch is idempotent and content dedup catches the duplicate page.

questions.prompt: After a week, **30% of your crawl budget** has gone to a single site with URLs like `/events?date=2031-04-17&session=8f3a…`, and many of those pages look almost identical. Diagnose what's happening and list the defenses you would add.
questions.hint: Two separate problems: infinite URL spaces, and near-identical content.
keyPoints: It's a crawler trap: an effectively infinite URL space (calendar dates, session IDs) generating endless 'new' URLs
Normalization should strip session-like parameters so equivalent URLs dedupe
Cap pages per host per crawl cycle, URL length and depth, and lower priority for hosts with low new-content yield
Detect near-duplicate pages with a similarity fingerprint like SimHash (or exact duplicates with a content hash) and stop following links from duplicate pages
Monitor per-host budget/yield metrics and alert on anomalies
questions.answer:
**Diagnosis: a crawler trap.** The site has an effectively **infinite URL space**: every calendar page links to the next date (up to 2031 and beyond), and the `session=` parameter makes the *same* page look like a new URL on every visit. The URL-seen filter never says "seen", so the frontier fills with this one host.

**Defenses**
1. **Normalize harder.** Strip session-like parameters (`session`, `sid`, `jsessionid`, `utm_*`) and sort the rest before the seen-check, so equivalent URLs collapse to one.
2. **Budgets and limits.** Cap pages per host per crawl cycle (e.g. 50,000), maximum URL length (e.g. 2,000 chars) and maximum link depth from the seed. Lower a host's priority when its **yield** (new, unique content per fetch) is low.
3. **Content dedup.** Hash each body (SHA-256) to catch exact duplicates, and use **SimHash** (a fingerprint where similar pages differ in only a few bits) to catch near-duplicates such as the same page with a different date header. Don't follow links from duplicate pages, which cuts off the maze.
4. **Monitoring.** Track per-host share of budget and unique-content ratio; alert when one host passes, say, 1% of fetches or its many URLs keep producing the same content hashes.
